assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines the magic-wavelength lattice idea with strontium and related clocks, giving fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. It is a clean, original instrument-driven advance that redefined precision timekeeping and enabled tests of relativity, searches for varying constants and relativistic geodesy. As an experimentalist I value that it is a measurement capability with broad downstream use.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and realized the first lattice clock; Jun Ye drove it to record accuracy and many-body clock physics. A two-person prize is natural. Other groups (for example NIST, SYRTE, PTB) also contributed, but I judge the decisive credit to be well captured by these two.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently across several laboratories and species, with international comparisons and talk of a redefinition of the second. Recognition is timely and the field is stable. The 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured adjacent frequency-comb and ion-control work, so overlap is a consideration but not a barrier.
uncertainties: I rely on recalled history of who first proposed and realized the magic-wavelength scheme and have not verified it here.
The committee may weigh whether Ye's frequency-comb ties to the 2005 prize reduce novelty, though the clock itself is distinct.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube instrumented a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice and in 2013 reported a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos, later tied to the blazar TXS 0506+056 and to the Galactic plane. This opened neutrino astronomy and addresses the origin of cosmic rays, a topic close to my own field. The detector engineering and the scientific payoff are both significant.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led the project, and Karle was a central driver of construction and detector design. The collaboration involves hundreds of people, and AMANDA and earlier DUMAND and Baikal pioneers have a legitimate claim to part of the credit. A prize to Halzen and Karle alone would be defensible but would leave real allocation questions open.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is confirmed through several analyses and by other detectors at lower significance; the source identifications are fewer and still developing. Maturity is solid for the discovery of the flux but still evolving for the sources.
uncertainties: Allocation of credit among IceCube, AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers is unresolved.
Source associations beyond TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are still maturing; I cannot verify the latest significances.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators represent a conceptual shift in classifying band structure, with theoretical prediction followed by decisive transport observation in HgTe quantum wells. The idea has become central to condensed matter physics, with spin-orbit-driven edge and surface states and links to spintronics and topological materials.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 theory, Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from this credited set and of the ARPES observers (Hasan, Shen and others) is a real allocation problem; the supplied three-name set is workable but not obviously complete.
assessment.maturity: Extremely well confirmed across materials and techniques over nearly two decades. The 2016 prize on topological phases and transitions lowers marginal novelty somewhat, but this is distinct enough in my judgment.
uncertainties: Credit boundaries among theory proposers (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang), Kane and Mele, and the experimental teams are contested.
Overlap with the 2016 topological-phase prize is a possible committee concern.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Correcting spherical aberration in electron lenses overcame a limit that had stood since Scherzer's 1936 theorem, bringing atomic-resolution imaging, picometre atom positioning and chemical mapping into routine use in materials science. A real instrumentation breakthrough with broad impact on physics, materials and nanoscience.
assessment.attribution: Rose provided the theoretical design of the corrector, Haider and Urban built and demonstrated the working corrector in a TEM, and Urban extended it to the scanning-probe-like use in materials. This is a natural three-way split with relatively clear roles, though the credit of Krivanek and others on STEM correctors is a competing claim.
assessment.maturity: The technique is widely deployed commercially and fully confirmed in practice; the discovery dates to the late 1990s so recognition is overdue rather than premature. Kavli and Wolf recognition supports the picture.
uncertainties: The Krivanek STEM corrector development may need to be considered alongside the TEM corrector credit.
Committee may judge it closer to chemistry or instrumentation than physics, though electron optics is a physics subject.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: X-ray free-electron lasers based on SASE deliver femtosecond, extremely bright coherent X-ray pulses and have transformed structural biology, ultrafast chemistry and matter under extreme conditions. A landmark accelerator and instrumentation achievement.
assessment.attribution: Pellegrini was the central proponent of the LCLS-type SASE concept, Rossbach led the TESLA test facility and European XFEL line, and Ishikawa led SACLA. The theoretical lineage (Bonifacio, Pellegrini, Narducci; Kondratenko and Saldin) and the many accelerator builders make a clean three-person allocation contestable.
assessment.maturity: Operational at multiple facilities with many verified results; mature. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Credit for the SASE theory versus the facility builders is disputed and I cannot settle it from the supplied information.
Subject may be considered closer to accelerator engineering than a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon microstrip and pixel detectors made precise vertexing and charm and beauty tagging possible, and are now foundational in collider experiments including those that discovered the Higgs boson. Having worked with silicon detectors in space and balloon instruments, I value this technology as an enabling instrument with large impact across particle, astroparticle and medical physics.
assessment.attribution: Kemmer introduced planar processing for detectors, Heijne developed pixel and hybrid concepts and readout, Parker developed microstrip and later pixel devices. Many other contributors (Rancoita, Holl, Lutz, CERN RD19 groups) make the allocation of three credits uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Fully established across several decades of use. Recognition could be considered overdue, though a prize for a detector technology without a single dramatic discovery is a harder narrative for the committee.
uncertainties: Allocation among a larger community of detector developers is unclear.
I have a professional familiarity with silicon detectors, which may bias my enthusiasm; I note it as a potential perspective effect.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Predicted flat bands at a magic twist angle, followed by observation of correlated insulator and superconducting states in magic-angle bilayer graphene, opened twistronics and a very active field of tunable correlated matter. A striking prediction-to-experiment story.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the continuum-model prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the experimental discovery of correlated states and superconductivity. Related contributions (Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Young, Yankowitz, Kim and others, plus Santos and Peres, and Lopes dos Santos) leave credit unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by multiple laboratories, but the interpretation of the superconductivity and correlated phases is still debated, so the field is young. Recognition might be somewhat early.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity and other phases is unresolved.
Allocation among early theoretical and experimental contributors is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* are a remarkable experimental feat, combining global VLBI, calibration and imaging methods to test general relativity in the strong-field regime. Visually and scientifically compelling, though the physics extracted so far is largely confirmatory.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed imaging the shadow, Doeleman led the EHT mm-VLBI development and Zensus led the European and MPIfR efforts. The EHT is a collaboration of over 300 people and the three-name limit makes a fair prize hard; other leaders (Ohm, Hirabayashi, Broderick, Loeb) have claims.
assessment.maturity: Two images and polarization follow-up are consistent, but the program is young and new observations may revise interpretation; arguably it is a little early.
uncertainties: The three-person limit conflicts with the collective nature of the achievement.
Independent confirmation beyond the EHT collaboration is limited.
